Estimate how much condo (HO-6) insurance you need, from walls-in dwelling and personal property to loss assessment and liability, plus an estimated premium for your state.

The post Condo Insurance Calculator: How Much HO-6 Coverage Do You Need? appeared first on Coverage Estimate.
item.content:encoded:
A Condo Insurance Calculator helps unit owners answer two questions that most insurance quotes skip over: how much HO-6 coverage do you actually need, and roughly what should that coverage cost in your state? It does not replace a quote from a licensed agent, but it gives you a clear starting point before you shop, renew, or sign the closing documents on a new unit.

That starting point matters.

A condo policy is not a smaller version of a homeowners policy. It is designed to fit around the association’s master policy, and the right limits depend on what that master policy leaves out. Two owners with identical units in different buildings can need very different coverage simply because their associations insure the building differently.

Many owners never check. They accept the default limits on a quote, assume the HOA covers the rest, and find out after a burst pipe or a hurricane that the interior of their unit, or a large special assessment, was their responsibility all along.

This guide explains how to use the calculator below, what each part of an HO-6 policy covers, how the coverage limits and premium estimate are calculated, and how average condo insurance costs compare by state.

Use the Condo Insurance Calculator

The calculator below estimates recommended limits for each major part of a condo unit owner’s policy and a preliminary annual premium range.

It can help estimate:

  • Coverage A: dwelling or walls-in coverage
  • Coverage C: personal property
  • Coverage D: loss of use
  • Loss assessment coverage
  • Coverage E: personal liability
  • Your share of the HOA master policy deductible
  • An estimated annual and monthly premium compared with your state average

      How Much Condo Insurance Do I Need?

      For most unit owners, the answer comes down to five numbers:

      The calculator works through each of these using your unit size, finish level, master policy type, belongings, association details, and assets.

      What an HO-6 Policy Covers

      An HO-6 policy, also called condo insurance or a unit owner’s policy, covers the parts of your financial exposure that the association’s master policy does not.

      Coverage A: Dwelling or Walls-In Coverage

      Coverage A pays to repair or rebuild the parts of the unit you are responsible for. Depending on your association’s documents, that may include:

      • Interior drywall and paint
      • Flooring
      • Kitchen cabinets and countertops
      • Bathroom fixtures and vanities
      • Built-in appliances
      • Interior doors and trim
      • Electrical and plumbing fixtures inside the unit
      • Upgrades you or a previous owner installed

      This is usually the most misunderstood limit on a condo policy. It should be based on the cost to rebuild your interior, not the purchase price of the unit or its market value.

      Coverage C: Personal Property

      Coverage C protects belongings such as furniture, rugs, electronics, clothing, kitchenware, and artwork. Look for replacement cost coverage rather than actual cash value, which subtracts depreciation from claim payments.

      High-value items such as jewelry, firearms, collectibles, and fine art often have low sublimits and may need to be scheduled separately.

      Coverage D: Loss of Use

      If a covered loss makes your unit uninhabitable, loss of use pays for temporary housing, meals above your normal costs, and similar expenses. In a large building, repairs after a fire or hurricane can take many months, especially when the association must first settle its own claim.

      Loss Assessment Coverage

      When the association suffers a covered loss, it may pass part of the cost to owners through a special assessment. The most common example is the master policy deductible. Loss assessment coverage pays your share, subject to your policy terms.

      Many HO-6 policies include only $1,000 of loss assessment coverage by default. Higher limits are usually inexpensive to add.

      Coverage E: Personal Liability and Medical Payments

      Liability coverage protects you if someone is injured in your unit or if you accidentally damage another unit, for example when a washing machine hose fails and water travels to the units below.

      Bare Walls, Single Entity, and All-In Master Policies

      The single most important input in the calculator is what the HOA master policy covers. Your association’s declarations, bylaws, or insurance summary will usually describe it.

      If you are not sure which type applies, choose “Not sure” in the calculator. It will assume a bare-walls policy, which produces the most conservative Coverage A estimate. Ask the association manager or board for a copy of the master policy declarations to confirm.

      How the Calculator Works

      The calculator follows a simplified sequence for each coverage.

      Dwelling Coverage

      The calculator first estimates the cost to rebuild the unit’s interior from the studs in:

      Interior rebuild cost = unit square footage × finish cost per square foot × local cost adjustment

      The finish levels used are:

      • Standard or builder grade: $80 per square foot
      • Mid-range: $115 per square foot
      • High-end: $160 per square foot
      • Luxury or custom: $230 per square foot

      The local cost adjustment ranges from 0.9 for below-average construction markets to 1.3 for high-cost metro areas.

      The calculator then applies the share left to you under your master policy type: 100% for bare walls, 25% for single entity, and 10% for all-in. It adds any upgrades you have made and rounds up to the nearest $5,000, with a $10,000 minimum.

      Personal Property

      If you enter the value of your belongings, the calculator uses it. If you leave it blank, it estimates $25 per square foot, with a $25,000 minimum. A room-by-room home inventory will always be more accurate.

      Loss of Use

      When you enter a monthly rent for comparable temporary housing, the calculator recommends 12 months of that rent. Otherwise, it uses 40% of Coverage C, a common default on HO-6 policies.

      Loss Assessment

      The calculator divides the HOA master policy deductible by the number of units to estimate your share, adds a 25% buffer, and rounds up to a common coverage tier of $10,000, $25,000, $50,000, $75,000, or $100,000. If you leave these fields blank, it assumes a $25,000 deductible and 50 units.

      Actual assessments are allocated according to your association’s governing documents, often by ownership percentage rather than equal shares.

      Liability

      The recommendation is based on the assets you want to protect: $300,000 for under $300,000, $500,000 for $300,000 to $1 million, and $500,000 plus a $1 million umbrella policy above that.

      Premium Estimate

      The premium estimate starts with the average HO-6 premium for your state from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), adjusted upward by 25% to reflect rate increases since the most recent published data year. That figure is then scaled up or down based on how your recommended limits compare with a typical condo policy and adjusted for your deductible.

      The result is shown as a midpoint with a likely range of 20% above and below it. Insurers price individual buildings very differently, so actual quotes may fall outside that range.

      Example Condo Insurance Calculation

      Suppose an owner in Florida has the following:

      • 1,100 square foot unit
      • Mid-range finishes
      • Bare-walls master policy
      • $15,000 in kitchen upgrades
      • $40,000 in belongings
      • $2,400 monthly rent for comparable temporary housing
      • $750,000 HOA hurricane deductible shared by 60 units
      • $300,000 to $1 million in assets
      • $1,000 HO-6 deductible

      The interior rebuild cost is 1,100 × $115 = $126,500. Adding $15,000 in upgrades gives $141,500, which rounds up to $145,000 of Coverage A.

      Personal property is set at $40,000. Loss of use is 12 months × $2,400 = $28,800, rounded to $29,000.

      The owner’s share of the hurricane deductible is $750,000 ÷ 60 = $12,500. With a 25% buffer, that becomes $15,625, so the calculator recommends $25,000 of loss assessment coverage.

      Liability is set at $500,000.

      Because these limits are well above a typical condo policy and Florida’s average premium is the highest in the country, the estimated premium is about $2,180 per year, with a likely range of roughly $1,740 to $2,620.

      Click Load Example in the calculator to see these numbers.

      How Much Does Condo Insurance Cost?

      According to the NAIC, the national average HO-6 premium was $531 per year in its most recent published report, which covers 2021. Premiums have generally risen since then, particularly in states exposed to hurricanes and severe convective storms.

      The table below shows the average annual HO-6 premium reported by the NAIC for each state.

      Source: National Association of Insurance Commissioners, Dwelling Fire, Homeowners Owner-Occupied, and Homeowners Tenant and Condominium/Cooperative Unit Owner’s Insurance Report. State averages reflect the coverage owners actually purchased, so they are a benchmark, not a quote.

      Factors That Affect Condo Insurance Premiums

      Location and Catastrophe Exposure

      Coastal wind, hail, wildfire, and freeze risk drive the largest differences between states and even between ZIP codes in the same state.

      Coverage Limits

      Higher Coverage A and Coverage C limits increase the premium. Under a bare-walls master policy, Coverage A is often the largest single driver of cost.

      Deductible

      Raising your deductible from $1,000 to $2,500 or $5,000 lowers the premium, but you will pay more out of pocket on every claim.

      Building Age and Construction

      Older plumbing and electrical systems, frame construction, and buildings without sprinklers can increase rates. Newer buildings with fire-resistive construction and modern wind protection often qualify for lower premiums.

      Claims History and Rating Factors

      Prior claims, and in many states a credit-based insurance score, affect individual pricing.

      Endorsements

      Water backup coverage, scheduled personal property, higher loss assessment limits, and building ordinance coverage add to the premium but can close important gaps.

      Loss Assessment Coverage: The Most Overlooked Limit

      Master policy deductibles have grown sharply, especially in Florida, along the Gulf Coast, and in hail-prone states. Many associations now carry windstorm or hurricane deductibles of 2% to 5% of the building’s insured value.

      On a $30 million building, a 5% hurricane deductible is $1.5 million. Spread across 60 units, that is $25,000 per owner before the master policy pays anything.

      Two details deserve careful review:

      • The limit. A default $1,000 of loss assessment coverage does not come close to a share of a percentage deductible.
      • The deductible assessment sublimit. Some policies limit how much of the loss assessment coverage applies to assessments for the master policy deductible, sometimes to $1,000 or less, unless you add an endorsement.

      Ask your agent specifically whether your loss assessment coverage will pay your share of the association’s deductible, and up to what amount.

      Common Condo Insurance Mistakes

      Insuring the Purchase Price

      The price of a condo includes land value, location, amenities, and market demand. None of that has anything to do with the cost to rebuild your interior.

      Assuming the HOA Covers Everything Inside

      Under a bare-walls policy, the association may not pay for a single cabinet, floor tile, or sheet of drywall inside your unit.

      Forgetting Improvements

      Renovated kitchens, upgraded flooring, and new bathrooms are often excluded under single-entity master policies. If Coverage A was set when you bought the unit, it may not include later upgrades.

      Accepting the Default Loss Assessment Limit

      The default limit on many policies is far below a realistic share of a modern master deductible.

      Choosing Actual Cash Value

      Actual cash value coverage subtracts depreciation from claim payments. Replacement cost coverage costs more, but it pays to replace damaged items with new ones of similar kind and quality.

      Never Reviewing the Policy After Purchase

      Construction costs, master policy terms, and your belongings all change. Review your coverage at each renewal, after any renovation, and whenever the association changes its insurance program.

      Limitations of the Condo Insurance Calculator

      The calculator is a planning tool. It does not:

      • Read or interpret your association’s declarations or master policy
      • Account for specific insurer pricing, discounts, or underwriting rules
      • Include flood insurance, which standard HO-6 policies exclude
      • Include earthquake coverage
      • Evaluate scheduled jewelry, art, or collectibles
      • Determine how your association allocates assessments
      • Guarantee that any recommended limit is available or adequate

      Premium estimates are derived from statewide averages and simplified assumptions. Treat them as a benchmark for comparing quotes, not as a price you will be offered.

      Frequently Asked Questions

      What is a good amount of condo insurance coverage?

      There is no single number. Most owners should have enough Coverage A to rebuild the interior items the master policy excludes, enough Coverage C to replace their belongings, at least $300,000 in liability coverage, and loss assessment coverage that exceeds their share of the master policy deductible.

      Is condo insurance required?

      State law generally does not require it, but most mortgage lenders and many association bylaws do.

      Does condo insurance cover water damage?

      Most HO-6 policies cover sudden and accidental water damage, such as a burst pipe. Gradual leaks, maintenance issues, and flooding from outside are usually excluded. Water backup from drains often requires an endorsement.

      Does an HO-6 policy cover the building?

      No. The association’s master policy covers the building structure and common areas. The HO-6 covers your interior, belongings, liability, and your share of certain assessments.

      How much is condo insurance per month?

      Based on NAIC data, the national average is about $44 per month, but costs range from roughly $23 per month in the lowest-cost states to more than $85 per month in Florida, before recent rate increases.

      Final Thoughts

      The right condo insurance policy starts with understanding what the association already covers. Once you know the master policy type and deductible, the remaining limits are straightforward to estimate.

      Use the Condo Insurance Calculator to build a preliminary coverage worksheet, then compare it with your current declarations page or with quotes from licensed agents. If the results show a large gap in dwelling or loss assessment coverage, review your association’s documents and discuss the numbers with an insurance professional before your next renewal.

      If you are on the board and want to confirm the building itself is properly insured, start with our Condo Replacement Cost Calculator.

A home insurance deductible calculator answers two questions your declarations page does not spell out: how much would you actually pay if you filed a claim today, and is the deductible you chose the right one for your budget? It turns percentage hurricane and wind deductibles into real dollars, shows how a claim splits between you and the insurer, and compares the deductible options on your quote by break-even time and expected cost.

Those answers are worth having before a storm, not after one.

Most homeowners remember their deductible as a single number, often $1,000 or $2,500. Many policies, especially in coastal and hail-prone areas, carry a second or third deductible that applies only to certain causes of loss and is written as a percentage of the dwelling limit. A 2% hurricane deductible sounds small until you multiply it by a $350,000 dwelling limit and realize it is $7,000.

The other half of the decision is the premium. Raising your deductible lowers what you pay each year, but it raises what you pay when something goes wrong. Whether that trade makes sense depends on how much you save, how often you expect to claim, and how much cash you could produce on short notice.

This guide explains how home insurance deductibles work, the difference between flat and percentage deductibles, how hurricane and wind/hail deductibles differ, and how the calculator below decides which option has the lowest expected cost.

Use the Home Insurance Deductible Calculator

The calculator below has two parts. Part 1 works out the deductible on a specific claim, so it also works as a hurricane deductible calculator or wind deductible calculator when your policy uses a percentage deductible. Part 2 compares two or three deductible options from your quote.

It can help estimate:

  • Which deductible applies to a claim, based on the cause of loss
  • The dollar amount of a percentage hurricane, named storm, or wind/hail deductible
  • What the insurer would pay and what you would pay out of pocket
  • Annual premium savings and extra risk per claim for each deductible option
  • Break-even years for a higher deductible
  • Expected total cost of each option over a period you choose
  • Whether each deductible fits within your emergency savings

      How Home Insurance Deductibles Work

      A deductible is the part of a covered loss you pay before the insurance company pays. If a covered fire causes $5,000 of damage and your deductible is $1,000, the insurer pays $4,000 and you absorb the first $1,000.

      Three points cause most of the confusion.

      First, the deductible comes off the covered loss. You usually do not mail the insurer a check; the adjuster calculates the covered damage, subtracts the deductible, and pays the rest, subject to the policy limit and other terms.

      Second, if the damage is less than the deductible, the insurer pays nothing. A $1,800 repair under a $2,500 deductible is entirely yours, whether you file a claim or not.

      Third, most homeowners deductibles apply per occurrence. Each separate event, such as a kitchen fire in March and a burst pipe in October, usually carries its own deductible. How a policy treats a hurricane season with more than one storm varies by state and policy; some apply a hurricane deductible once per season or calendar year, while others apply it to each storm. Your policy wording controls.

      Flat Deductibles vs Percentage Deductibles

      A homeowners policy can express a deductible in two ways.

      A flat deductible is a fixed dollar amount, such as $1,000, $2,500, or $5,000. You know exactly what it is, and it does not change when your coverage limit changes.

      A percentage deductible is a percentage of the dwelling limit, which is Coverage A on your declarations page. It is not a percentage of the claim. A 2% deductible on a home insured for $350,000 is $7,000 whether the damage is $10,000 or $100,000.

      Percentage deductibles grow automatically when your dwelling limit grows. If your insurer raises Coverage A at renewal to keep up with construction costs, a 2% deductible rises with it. That is one reason to know your real rebuilding cost. Our Home Replacement Cost Calculator can help you check whether your dwelling limit is realistic.

      Hurricane, Named Storm, and Wind/Hail Deductibles

      Many policies carry a standard deductible plus one or more deductibles that apply only to certain weather events.

      All-Other-Perils Deductible

      The all-other-perils (AOP) deductible applies to most covered losses that are not subject to a special deductible: fire, theft, lightning, sudden water damage, and similar events. It is usually a flat dollar amount, though some insurers offer it as a percentage.

      Hurricane and Named Storm Deductibles

      A hurricane or named storm deductible applies to damage caused by a qualifying storm. What makes a storm qualify, sometimes called the trigger, varies by state and by policy. Triggers can be tied to a hurricane watch or warning, a storm being named by the National Weather Service, or a storm reaching hurricane strength, and the window during which the deductible applies is also defined in the policy. The Insurance Information Institute describes hurricane deductibles as typically ranging from 1% to 5% of a home’s insured value, and some higher-risk areas can see more.

      Wind and Hail Deductibles

      A wind/hail or windstorm deductible applies to damage from wind or hail, often regardless of whether a named storm is involved. These are common in states with frequent hail and severe thunderstorms, and they are also usually written as a percentage of Coverage A. Some policies have only a wind/hail deductible, which then applies to hurricane wind damage as well.

      How to Use the Calculator

      Part 1: Deductible on a Claim

      Dwelling limit (Coverage A). Enter the limit from your declarations page. Percentage deductibles are calculated from this number.

      All-other-perils deductible. Choose flat dollar amount or percentage, then enter the figure from your declarations page.

      Hurricane / named storm deductible. Enter the percentage, or leave it blank or at 0 if your policy has none.

      Wind / hail deductible. Enter the percentage, or leave it blank or at 0 if your policy has none.

      Sample claim amount. Enter the covered damage before the deductible.

      Cause of loss. Choose fire, water, theft, or other; wind or hail; or hurricane or named storm. This decides which deductible applies.

      Part 2: Compare Deductible Options

      Options A, B, and C. For each option on your quote, enter the all-other-perils deductible and the annual premium. Option C is optional.

      Emergency savings. Enter the cash you could use for a deductible without borrowing. This field is optional but powers the emergency-fund check.

      Years to compare and claim frequency. Under Comparison Assumptions, choose how many years to compare and how often you expect to file a claim. If left blank, the calculator uses 10 years and one claim every 10 years.

      How the Calculator Works

      Which Deductible Applies

      The calculator converts each deductible to dollars:

      Percentage deductible = Coverage A × percentage

      A percentage deductible that works out to less than your all-other-perils deductible is raised to the all-other-perils amount, and the results note when that happens. Many policies set a minimum dollar amount for percentage deductibles, but the exact rule varies, so check your declarations.

      It then picks the deductible based on the cause of loss:

      • Fire, water, theft, or other: the all-other-perils deductible
      • Wind or hail: the wind/hail deductible if you entered one; otherwise the all-other-perils deductible
      • Hurricane or named storm: the hurricane deductible if you entered one; otherwise the wind/hail deductible; otherwise the all-other-perils deductible

      Insurer Payment and Out-of-Pocket Cost

      Insurer payment = claim amount − deductible, never less than zero and never more than the Coverage A limit.

      Your out-of-pocket = claim amount − insurer payment

      The calculator also shows the deductible as a share of the claim, which makes it easy to see how much of a mid-sized loss a percentage deductible absorbs.

      Comparing Deductible Options

      The option with the lowest deductible is the baseline. For every other option:

      Annual savings = baseline premium − option premium

      Extra risk per claim = option deductible − baseline deductible

      Break-even years = extra risk per claim ÷ annual savings

      Break-even years tells you how many claim-free years it takes for the premium savings to cover the extra deductible on one claim. If an option has a higher deductible but does not cost less, the calculator shows “Never” and flags the quote for a second look.

      The expected cost of each option over the comparison period is:

      Expected claims = years ÷ claim interval

      Expected total cost = (annual premium × years) + (expected claims × deductible)

      The calculator assumes every claim exceeds the deductible, so each claim costs you the full deductible, and it holds premiums flat over the period. It recommends the option with the lowest expected total cost; if two options are within $1, it picks the lower deductible.

      Emergency-Fund Check

      When you enter emergency savings, the calculator flags any recommended deductible larger than 50% of that amount, and it flags a percentage storm deductible from Part 1 the same way. A deductible larger than your entire savings is shown as a higher-priority warning. The 50% threshold is a planning choice, not an industry rule: it leaves room for the other costs that tend to arrive with a claim, such as temporary repairs, a hotel night, or items your policy does not cover.

      Example Home Insurance Deductible Calculation

      Suppose a homeowner has the following:

      • $350,000 dwelling limit (Coverage A)
      • $1,000 flat all-other-perils deductible
      • 2% hurricane deductible
      • No separate wind/hail deductible
      • $18,000 of covered damage from a hurricane
      • A renewal quote with three options: $1,000 deductible for $3,200 a year, $2,500 for $2,950, and $5,000 for $2,750
      • $12,000 in emergency savings
      • A 10-year comparison with one claim expected every 10 years

      Part 1. The hurricane deductible is 2% × $350,000 = $7,000. The insurer pays $18,000 − $7,000 = $11,000, and the homeowner pays $7,000, which is 38.9% of the claim. The $1,000 deductible would apply only to non-storm losses.

      Part 2. Option A is the baseline because it has the lowest deductible.

      Option B has the lowest expected cost, $32,000, which is $1,000 less than Option A over 10 years. Option C saves the most each year, but at one claim per decade its larger deductible eats most of that saving.

      The status block reads Storm Deductible Strains Savings. Option B’s $2,500 deductible is 21% of the homeowner’s savings, well within the 50% check. The $7,000 hurricane deductible, however, would use 58% of savings. On many policies, choosing a different all-other-perils deductible does not change the hurricane deductible, so this homeowner should plan for that $7,000 separately.

      Click Load Example in the calculator to see these numbers.

      When Raising Your Deductible Makes Sense

      Should I raise my deductible? The calculator gives you the math, but the answer usually comes down to three tests.

      The Break-Even Is Shorter Than Your Claim Interval

      If a higher deductible pays for itself in six claim-free years and you expect to claim about once a decade, it is likely to come out ahead. If the break-even is 12 years and you have filed two claims in the last five, it probably will not.

      You Can Pay the Higher Deductible Without Borrowing

      A deductible you cannot afford is not a savings. If paying it would mean a credit card balance or delayed repairs that let damage spread, the lower premium is a false economy.

      You Would Not File Small Claims Anyway

      Many homeowners avoid filing small claims because claims history can affect future premiums and eligibility, depending on the insurer and the state. If you would pay a $2,000 repair yourself regardless, a $1,000 deductible may be protecting you against claims you will never file.

      Raising a deductible makes less sense when savings are thin or when the quote shows only a small premium difference for a much larger deductible.

      Small Claims and Your Deductible

      When damage is only slightly above your deductible, the insurer’s payment is small, and the claim still goes on your record. A $3,000 claim under a $2,500 deductible pays $500.

      Before filing a small claim, get a repair estimate, compare it with your deductible, and consider whether the net payment is worth a claim on your history. That said, do not underestimate damage that is hard to see. Water that has reached subfloors or wall cavities, or hail damage across a full roof, is often larger than it looks at first. For roof claims in particular, how the policy values an older roof can matter as much as the deductible; our Roof Depreciation Calculator shows how age can reduce a roof payment.

      Deductibles and Claim Payments

      The deductible is only one of several deductions that can stand between the damage and your check. If your policy pays actual cash value for some items, depreciation is subtracted as well, and the deductible is typically applied on top of it. Our Actual Cash Value Calculator explains how depreciation affects those payments.

      On a large loss, the order of deductions and the policy limit matter. The calculator applies the deductible to the covered damage and caps the insurer’s payment at the Coverage A limit. Real claims can also involve separate limits for other structures, personal property, and additional living expenses, each with its own rules.

      Common Deductible Mistakes

      Not Knowing You Have a Percentage Deductible

      Many homeowners learn about their hurricane or wind/hail deductible after the storm. Read the deductible section of your declarations page, not just the first number.

      Comparing Premiums Without Comparing Risk

      A quote that saves $450 a year with a deductible $4,000 higher needs about nine claim-free years to break even. Look at both numbers together.

      Raising the Deductible Past Your Savings

      The right deductible is one you could pay next month without hardship.

      Limitations of the Home Insurance Deductible Calculator

      The calculator is a planning tool. It does not:

      • Read or interpret your policy, endorsements, or declarations page
      • Decide whether a storm meets your policy’s hurricane or named storm trigger
      • Account for state rules on how deductibles are applied, disclosed, or limited
      • Handle per-season or calendar-year hurricane deductibles across multiple storms
      • Include flood or earthquake deductibles, which are written under separate coverage
      • Model depreciation, coverage exclusions, or sublimits
      • Predict how often you will file a claim or how premiums will change

      Claim frequency is your own assumption. Treat the expected-cost comparison as a way to frame the decision, not as a forecast.

      Frequently Asked Questions

      How is a hurricane deductible calculated?

      A percentage hurricane deductible is usually the percentage multiplied by your dwelling (Coverage A) limit. A 2% deductible on a $350,000 dwelling limit is $7,000. Some policies set a minimum dollar amount, and some write the hurricane deductible as a flat amount instead. Your declarations page shows which applies.

      Is a wind deductible the same as a hurricane deductible?

      Not always. A hurricane or named storm deductible applies only to storms that meet the policy’s trigger. A wind/hail deductible can apply to any wind or hail damage, including ordinary thunderstorms. Some policies have one, some have both, and some have neither.

      Is a higher deductible worth it?

      It can be, when the premium savings recover the extra deductible faster than you expect to file claims and when you could pay the higher amount from savings. Use the break-even years and expected-cost results in the calculator to test your own quote.

      Does the deductible apply to every claim?

      In most policies, yes, each covered occurrence has its own deductible. Hurricane deductibles are sometimes applied once per season or year rather than per storm, depending on the state and policy.

      What happens if the damage is less than my deductible?

      The insurer pays nothing, and you cover the full repair cost. Many homeowners choose not to file in that situation, but if you are unsure how large the damage is, get an estimate first.

      Final Thoughts

      A deductible is easy to overlook when you buy a policy and impossible to ignore when you file a claim. Knowing the dollar amount of every deductible you carry, especially percentage storm deductibles, is the first step toward making sure a claim does not become a financial emergency.

      Use the Home Insurance Deductible Calculator to convert your deductibles into dollars, then compare the options on your next renewal quote with the break-even and expected-cost results. If you are facing a claim and are unsure which deductible applies or how the payment was calculated, review your policy with a licensed professional or contact us to talk through the numbers.

A roof depreciation calculator helps homeowners answer the question that matters most after a hail or windstorm: how much will the insurance company actually pay to replace the roof? The answer is rarely the full replacement cost. Roof age, the settlement terms in your policy, and your deductible all reduce the check, sometimes dramatically.

That gap surprises people.

A roof that costs $15,000 to replace can produce a first payment of under $1,000 when the roof is middle-aged and the policy carries a percentage wind and hail deductible. Whether the rest of the money is paid later depends on whether the policy settles roofs at replacement cost, at actual cash value, or on a roof payment schedule.

This guide explains how to use the calculator below, how insurers depreciate roofs, the difference between RCV, ACV, and roof payment schedules, how roof age is determined, and what to do when the insurer’s numbers do not match yours.

Use the Roof Depreciation Calculator

The calculator below works through a roof insurance claim the way most claim estimates are structured, from replacement cost to the payment you can expect.

It can help estimate:

  • Replacement cost value (RCV) of the roof
  • Depreciation in dollars and as a percentage
  • Actual cash value (ACV) after depreciation
  • The deductible applied, including percentage wind and hail deductibles
  • The initial payment and any recoverable depreciation
  • The total payment if the roof is replaced
  • Your out-of-pocket cost and the roof’s estimated remaining life

      Ask About a Roof Claim Review

      Preliminary estimate only: This calculator provides a general planning estimate based solely on the information entered by the user and simplified assumptions. It is not an insurance claim determination, appraisal, roofing estimate, coverage opinion, legal opinion, insurance advice, or guarantee of claim payment. Material service lives and cost-per-square figures are general planning ranges; actual depreciation, settlement terms, deductibles, and coverage depend on your policy wording, endorsements, the insurer’s estimate, local pricing, and the laws of your state. Review your policy and consult a licensed insurance professional or attorney about your specific claim.

      Your entries are calculated locally in your browser and are not transmitted or stored by this tool.

      The calculator processes entries locally in your browser. The information you enter is not transmitted or stored. Results are a preliminary planning estimate, not a claim determination, roofing estimate, or coverage opinion.

      What Is Roof Depreciation?

      Depreciation is the loss in value of a roof as it ages and wears. An insurer that pays actual cash value starts with what it would cost to replace the roof today, then subtracts depreciation to reflect the portion of the roof’s useful life that has already been used up.

      The basic relationship is simple:

      Actual cash value = replacement cost value − depreciation

      Most roof estimates calculate depreciation on a straight-line basis. If a roof covering is expected to last 25 years and it is 12 years old, it has used about 48% of its life, so 48% of the replacement cost is deducted. Adjusters may adjust that figure for condition, and many estimates cap depreciation at a maximum percentage so that even a very old roof retains some value.

      How depreciation affects your payment depends on the settlement terms in your policy, which is why the calculator asks for the settlement type separately from age and material.

      RCV vs. ACV vs. Roof Payment Schedules

      Roof coverage generally falls into one of three settlement structures. Your declarations page and any roof endorsement will tell you which one applies. Some policies use one basis for wind and hail damage and another for other perils, so read both.

      Replacement Cost With Recoverable Depreciation

      Under a replacement cost policy, the insurer typically pays in two stages. The first check is the actual cash value minus your deductible. The depreciation that was withheld, often called recoverable depreciation or holdback, is released after the roof is replaced and you provide the final invoice or other proof of completion.

      Your total payment if you replace the roof is the full replacement cost minus the deductible. Policies usually set a deadline for completing the replacement and claiming the holdback, and the time allowed varies by policy and state.

      Actual Cash Value Only

      Some policies, and some roof endorsements, pay only actual cash value for the roof. The depreciation is never paid back, even if you replace the roof. On an older roof, this can leave a large gap between the claim payment and the contractor’s price.

      Roof Payment Schedules

      A roof payment schedule replaces the depreciation calculation with a table. The policy lists the percentage of replacement cost the insurer will pay for roofs of a given age, and sometimes a given material. A newer roof may receive most of its replacement cost, while an older roof may receive a small fraction. Like ACV, the reduction is not recoverable.

      Schedules differ by insurer and endorsement, so the calculator’s default percentages are illustrative only. Replace them with the figures in your policy.

      How to Use Each Input

      Roofing Material

      Choose the roof covering on the damaged slopes. Each material shows a general industry range for expected service life, and the calculator uses the midpoint of that range unless you enter an override. If your claim estimate lists a specific life expectancy, enter it in the advanced options.

      Roof Age and Condition

      Enter the roof’s age in years as of the date of loss. The condition setting adjusts effective age: a roof in better-than-typical condition is treated as 85% of its actual age, a typical roof as 100%, and a worn or poorly maintained roof as 115%. Condition does not apply to roof payment schedules, which use actual age.

      Roof Size

      Enter the roof area in squares or square feet. One roofing square equals 100 square feet of roof surface. This is roof surface, not floor area, and is usually larger because of pitch and overhangs. Use a measurement report or an estimate’s square count when you have one.

      Replacement Cost per Square or Contractor Estimate

      The cost per square fills in automatically with a typical planning value for the selected material, including tear-off of one layer. Override it with your local price. If you have a contractor estimate or the insurer’s estimate, enter the total instead. It will be used as the replacement cost value and will include items such as underlayment, flashing, drip edge, ventilation, permits, and overhead and profit if they are in that estimate.

      Settlement Type and Deductible

      Choose the settlement type from your policy. For the deductible, choose a flat dollar amount or a percentage of dwelling coverage. Percentage deductibles are common for wind and hail in many regions. A 2% deductible on a home with $350,000 of dwelling coverage is $7,000, regardless of the size of the roof claim.

      Advanced Options

      The maximum depreciation defaults to 80%, and the waste allowance defaults to 10% of measured squares. Both are planning assumptions, not standards. Insurers, estimating software, and individual adjusters use different caps and waste factors, and complex roofs with many hips and valleys usually need more waste than simple gables.

      How the Calculator Works

      The calculator follows these steps.

      Replacement Cost Value

      When you enter a roof size and cost per square:

      Priced squares = measured squares × (1 + waste allowance)

      RCV = priced squares × replacement cost per square

      When you enter a contractor estimate, that amount is used as RCV and the size, cost per square, and waste allowance are not used for pricing.

      Depreciation and ACV

      For replacement cost and ACV settlements:

      Effective age = roof age × condition factor (0.85, 1.00, or 1.15)

      Depreciation % = effective age ÷ expected life, limited to the maximum depreciation cap

      Depreciation = RCV × depreciation %

      ACV = RCV − depreciation

      For a roof payment schedule, the calculator finds the age band for the roof’s actual age (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, or 20 or more years) and uses that schedule percentage as the payment basis. The reduction from RCV is shown in place of depreciation.

      Payments

      The deductible is taken from the first payment:

      Initial payment = ACV − deductible (not less than $0)

      Under replacement cost settlement:

      Total payment if replaced = RCV − deductible (not less than $0)

      Recoverable depreciation = total payment if replaced − initial payment

      Under ACV or a roof schedule, the total payment equals the initial payment and nothing is recoverable. In every case:

      Out-of-pocket if replaced = RCV − total payment

      Remaining life = expected life − effective age (not less than zero)

      The status block flags claims that may not exceed the deductible, large out-of-pocket gaps under ACV or schedule terms, and roofs at or beyond their expected life.

      Example Roof Depreciation Calculation

      Suppose a homeowner files a hail claim with these details:

      • Architectural asphalt shingles, 20 to 30 year range, 25-year midpoint
      • 12-year-old roof in typical condition
      • 25 squares measured
      • $550 per square installed, including tear-off
      • 10% waste allowance and 80% depreciation cap
      • Replacement cost settlement with recoverable depreciation
      • 2% wind and hail deductible on $350,000 of dwelling coverage

      Priced squares are 25 × 1.10 = 27.5. The replacement cost is 27.5 × $550 = $15,125.

      Depreciation is 12 ÷ 25 = 48%, well under the 80% cap. That is $15,125 × 48% = $7,260, leaving an ACV of $7,865.

      The deductible is 2% × $350,000 = $7,000. The initial payment is $7,865 − $7,000 = $865.

      After the roof is replaced and the final invoice is submitted, the insurer releases $7,260 of recoverable depreciation, for a total payment of $8,125. The homeowner’s out-of-pocket cost is the $7,000 deductible. The roof had an estimated 13 years of remaining life.

      Notice how small the first check is. Under an ACV-only policy, $865 would be the entire payment, and the homeowner would pay $14,260 toward a new roof.

      Click Load Example in the calculator to see these numbers.

      Typical Roof Lifespans and Replacement Costs

      The table below shows the general planning ranges the calculator uses. Actual lifespan depends on climate, installation quality, ventilation, and maintenance. Prices vary widely by region, roof complexity, and market conditions, especially after a major storm.

      These are planning figures, not quotes. An insurer’s estimate may use a different life expectancy for the same material, and that single assumption can change the depreciation by thousands of dollars.

      How Insurers Determine Roof Age

      Because depreciation is driven by age, roof age is one of the most frequently disputed facts in a roof claim. Insurers and adjusters commonly rely on:

      • Building permit records for the last reroof
      • Contractor invoices, contracts, and manufacturer warranty registrations
      • Home inspection reports from a purchase
      • Prior insurance applications, inspections, and underwriting photos
      • Aerial and satellite imagery showing when the roof changed
      • Physical indicators such as granule loss, shingle brittleness, and manufacturing details

      If the insurer lists an age older than you believe is correct, provide documentation. A permit or dated invoice is usually the strongest evidence. If only part of the roof was replaced, the ages of different slopes may differ.

      Cosmetic Damage and Matching

      Two policy issues often decide how much of the roof is covered at all.

      Cosmetic Damage Exclusions

      Some policies, particularly for metal roofs, include a cosmetic damage exclusion or endorsement. It generally excludes hail dents and marks that affect appearance but do not let water in or shorten the roof’s life. Whether this applies, and how “functional” damage is defined, depends entirely on your policy wording.

      Matching

      When only some slopes are damaged, the question becomes whether the insurer will pay to replace undamaged slopes so the roof matches. Treatment of matching varies by policy and by state. Some policies address it directly, and some limit it by endorsement. If replacement shingles are discontinued or the new material will not reasonably match, raise the issue with the adjuster and ask how the policy handles it.

      Steps to Document a Roof Claim

      Good documentation protects both the claim amount and the recoverable depreciation.

      • Photograph the roof, gutters, downspouts, siding, window screens, and outdoor equipment soon after the storm, with dates.
      • Note the date and time of the storm and save local weather reports or hail reports if available.
      • Make temporary repairs, such as tarping, to prevent further damage, and keep the receipts.
      • Gather proof of roof age: permits, invoices, warranties, and inspection reports.
      • Report the claim promptly and keep a log of every call, email, and inspection.
      • Request a copy of the insurer’s line-item estimate, including the life expectancy and depreciation used.
      • Get a detailed written estimate from a licensed roofer for comparison.
      • After replacement, submit the final invoice promptly to claim recoverable depreciation before any policy deadline.

      Common Roof Claim Mistakes

      Assuming the First Check Is the Final Payment

      Under replacement cost settlement, the first check is usually only ACV minus the deductible. The holdback comes later, but only if you replace the roof and follow the policy’s procedure.

      Missing the Recoverable Depreciation Deadline

      Policies commonly limit how long you have to complete repairs and claim withheld depreciation. Ask for the deadline in writing.

      Ignoring a Percentage Deductible

      A percentage deductible is based on dwelling coverage, not the size of the claim. On a high-value home, it can consume most of a modest roof claim.

      Accepting the Roof Age Without Checking

      An age error of a few years can shift depreciation by thousands of dollars. Verify the age in the estimate against your records.

      When to Get a Second Opinion

      If the numbers do not add up, you have options, and the right one depends on the size of the difference and the nature of the disagreement.

      Start by asking the adjuster to explain the estimate line by line and to reinspect with your roofer present. Many disagreements over missed slopes, accessories, or measurements are resolved this way.

      If the disagreement is over the amount of the loss, many property policies include an appraisal clause. Each side selects an appraiser, and an umpire resolves differences. Appraisal terms, costs, and whether appraisal applies to a given dispute depend on the policy and state law.

      A licensed public adjuster can prepare an independent estimate and handle the claim on your behalf, usually for a percentage of the settlement. Public adjuster licensing and fee rules vary by state. For disputes over coverage or claim handling, an attorney may be the appropriate professional. If you would like a second look at a roof claim, you can contact us.

      Limitations of the Roof Depreciation Calculator

      The calculator is a planning tool. It does not:

      • Determine whether the damage is covered or caused by a covered peril
      • Read your policy, endorsements, or roof payment schedule
      • Price individual line items such as decking, flashing, gutters, or code upgrades
      • Reflect a specific insurer’s depreciation tables or estimating software settings
      • Account for partial roof repairs, multiple layers, or steep-slope and high-roof charges
      • Determine matching obligations or the effect of a cosmetic damage exclusion
      • Guarantee any claim payment

      For a broader view of how depreciation affects other property, our Actual Cash Value Calculator applies the same principles to belongings and building components. To check whether your overall dwelling limit keeps pace with rebuilding costs, which also affects any percentage deductible, use the Home Replacement Cost Calculator.

      Frequently Asked Questions

      How much does insurance depreciate a roof per year?

      Under straight-line depreciation, the annual rate is 100% divided by the expected life. A roof with a 25-year expected life loses about 4% of its replacement cost value per year, and a 20-year roof about 5%.

      Will insurance pay for a 20-year-old roof?

      It depends on the policy. Under replacement cost settlement, a covered loss can still be paid at full replacement cost minus the deductible once the roof is replaced. Under ACV or a roof payment schedule, the payment on a 20-year-old asphalt roof may be a small fraction of replacement cost. Some insurers also restrict coverage for older roofs at renewal.

      What is recoverable depreciation on a roof claim?

      It is the depreciation withheld from the first payment under a replacement cost policy. It is paid after the roof is replaced and you submit proof of completion, subject to the policy’s time limit.

      Is the deductible taken out of the depreciation or the ACV?

      The deductible is normally subtracted from the first payment, which is based on ACV. If the deductible is larger than the ACV, the remaining deductible reduces what is recoverable later.

      How do I find my roof settlement type?

      Check the declarations page and look for roof surface payment schedule, actual cash value roof, or similar endorsements. If the wording is unclear, ask your agent or insurer for a written explanation.

      Final Thoughts

      A roof insurance claim payment is the product of a few numbers: replacement cost, roof age, expected life, settlement type, and deductible. Once you know them, the payment is predictable, and so are the surprises.

      Use the Roof Depreciation Calculator to build a preliminary roof claim worksheet, then compare it with the insurer’s estimate. If the age, life expectancy, square count, or settlement basis differ from yours, ask why, document your position, and consider a second opinion before accepting a settlement you do not understand.

A coinsurance calculator shows whether a property insurance policy carries enough limit to satisfy its coinsurance clause and, if it does not, how much a coinsurance penalty would cut a claim payment. It takes a few numbers from the declarations page and the loss, applies the same steps an adjuster uses, and shows how the loss is split between the insurer and the policyholder.

That split can be a surprise.

A coinsurance clause does not take effect when the policy is bought or renewed. It applies on the day of a loss, using the property value on that day. A building that was insured properly five years ago can be underinsured today simply because construction costs went up. When that happens, the insurer pays only part of even a small partial loss, and the owner pays the rest.

A quick note before going further: this tool is for coinsurance clauses in property insurance, which appear mostly in commercial property policies and in some dwelling and condominium association policies. It is not for health insurance coinsurance, where the word means the percentage of medical bills a patient pays after the deductible. The two concepts share a name and nothing else.

This guide covers how to use the calculator, how the penalty is calculated, worked examples at 80%, 90%, and 100%, and how to avoid a penalty.

Use the Coinsurance Calculator

The calculator below applies the coinsurance method found in the standard ISO commercial property form to your figures.

It can help estimate:

  • The amount of insurance the coinsurance clause requires
  • Your coinsurance ratio (limit carried divided by limit required)
  • Whether the requirement is met
  • The estimated insurer payment for a loss
  • The coinsurance penalty compared with a fully insured payment
  • Your total out-of-pocket cost: deductible, penalty, and any loss above the limit
  • The additional limit needed to meet the requirement

Property Claim Screening Tool

Coinsurance Calculator

      Preliminary estimate only: This calculator applies a simplified version of the coinsurance method used in common commercial property forms to the figures entered by the user. It is for property insurance coinsurance clauses, not health insurance. It is not an appraisal, claim adjustment, coverage opinion, legal opinion, insurance advice, or guarantee of any claim payment. Actual settlements depend on the exact policy wording, endorsements, valuation, deductibles, sublimits, exclusions, and how the property value and loss are documented. Review your declarations and policy forms and consult a licensed insurance professional or public adjuster about a specific claim.

      Your entries are calculated locally in your browser and are not transmitted or stored by this tool.

      The calculator processes entries locally in your browser. The information you enter is not transmitted or stored. Results are a preliminary screening estimate based on simplified assumptions, not a claim adjustment or coverage opinion.

      What Is a Coinsurance Clause?

      A coinsurance clause is a condition in a property policy that requires you to insure the property for at least a stated percentage of its value. The percentage, usually 80%, 90%, or 100%, appears on the declarations page next to the limit.

      If your limit meets that requirement at the time of loss, the insurer pays covered losses in full, minus the deductible, up to the limit. If your limit falls short, the insurer pays only a proportion of the loss. The shortfall you absorb is commonly called the coinsurance penalty.

      The clause exists because most property losses are partial. If owners could insure a $1,000,000 building for $400,000 and still collect in full on every partial loss, they would pay far less premium than owners who insure to value, for nearly the same protection. Coinsurance keeps the premium fair across policyholders by rewarding those who carry a limit close to the property’s true value. Underwriters and agents call this principle insurance to value.

      The Coinsurance Formula

      In the commonly used ISO Building and Personal Property Coverage Form (CP 00 10), the coinsurance condition sets out four steps when the limit is too low:

      • Multiply the value of the covered property at the time of loss by the coinsurance percentage. This is the insurance required.
      • Divide the limit of insurance by the insurance required. This is the coinsurance ratio.
      • Multiply the total amount of loss, before the deductible, by the ratio.
      • Subtract the deductible.

      The insurer pays that result or the limit of insurance, whichever is less. Written as one line:

      Payment = (Limit carried ÷ Insurance required) × Loss − Deductible, capped at the limit

      When the limit meets or exceeds the insurance required, the ratio is treated as 100%, so the payment is simply the loss minus the deductible, up to the limit.

      Where Coinsurance Clauses Appear

      Coinsurance is standard in commercial property policies covering buildings, business personal property, and business income. Condominium and homeowners association master policies are usually written on commercial property forms, so boards face the same requirement. Some dwelling fire policies used for rental properties include it as well.

      Standard homeowners policies work a little differently. Many, including the widely used ISO HO-3 form, do not have a coinsurance clause, but they include a similar insurance-to-value test in the loss settlement section. If the dwelling limit is at least 80% of the home’s full replacement cost at the time of loss, building losses are paid at replacement cost up to the limit. If it is less, the policy pays the greater of the actual cash value of the damage or a proportion of the replacement cost. The arithmetic is related, but this calculator models the commercial coinsurance clause, not that homeowners provision. Homeowners who want to check their dwelling limit can start with our Home Replacement Cost Calculator.

      How to Use the Calculator

      Policy Valuation Basis

      Choose replacement cost or actual cash value to match how your policy values the property. Coinsurance is measured on the same basis. If the policy settles losses at replacement cost, the property value used for coinsurance is its replacement cost. If it settles at actual cash value, the value is replacement cost minus depreciation. This selection only changes the guidance for the value field; the math is the same.

      Property Value at Time of Loss

      Enter what it would cost to rebuild or replace the covered property at the date of loss, on the basis you selected. For a building, that means construction cost, not market value, assessed value, or purchase price. Land is not part of it. If you are measuring actual cash value, our Actual Cash Value Calculator explains how depreciation is applied.

      This is the input that most often decides the outcome, and it is the one owners most often underestimate.

      Coinsurance Percentage

      Select 80%, 90%, or 100% from your declarations, or choose Custom for another whole number between 50 and 100. Each coverage can carry its own percentage, so use the one shown for the property you are testing.

      Limit of Insurance Carried

      Enter the limit for the property being tested, for example the building limit. Do not combine building and contents limits unless they are written as a single blanket limit.

      Amount of Loss

      Enter the covered loss before the deductible, measured on the same valuation basis. The calculator will not accept a loss larger than the property value.

      Deductible

      Enter the deductible in dollars. If your policy has a percentage deductible, such as a 2% wind deductible, convert it to dollars first. Enter 0 if there is none.

      Coinsurance Waived

      Check this box only if the declarations show an agreed value or a coinsurance waiver for this property, the agreed value period has not expired, and the limit is at least the agreed value. When checked, the calculator applies no penalty.

      How the Calculator Works

      The calculator follows the ISO CP 00 10 steps in this order:

      • Insurance required = property value × coinsurance percentage
      • Coinsurance ratio = limit carried ÷ insurance required, treated as 100% when the requirement is met or coinsurance is waived
      • Adjusted loss = amount of loss × coinsurance ratio
      • Insurer payment = adjusted loss − deductible, no less than $0 and no more than the limit

      It then compares that payment with what the same loss would pay with no coinsurance shortfall:

      • Payment if fully insured = loss − deductible, no less than $0 and no more than the limit
      • Coinsurance penalty = payment if fully insured − insurer payment
      • Loss above the limit = any part of the loss, after the deductible, that exceeds the limit
      • Total out-of-pocket = loss − insurer payment, which equals the deductible plus the penalty plus any loss above the limit
      • Additional limit needed = insurance required − limit carried, when positive

      The calculator also flags a thin margin when the limit meets the requirement by less than 10%. That threshold is a planning choice rather than an industry rule; it reflects the fact that values keep rising during a policy term while the limit usually stays fixed.

      Deductible Order: Why Policy Wording Controls

      The order of the deductible matters, and not every policy uses the same one. The ISO commercial property form applies the coinsurance ratio to the full loss first and subtracts the deductible last, and its deductible section confirms that the loss is first reduced for coinsurance. Some other forms, including some businessowners policies, subtract the deductible before applying the ratio. Manuscript and non-ISO forms may say something else again.

      Using the example below, the ISO order produces a payment of $161,667. Subtracting the deductible first would produce ($750,000 ÷ $900,000) × ($200,000 − $5,000) = $162,500. The gap is small with a $5,000 deductible, but it grows with large percentage deductibles. The exact wording in your policy always controls.

      Example Coinsurance Calculation

      Suppose a commercial building has:

      • Replacement cost at the time of loss: $1,000,000
      • Replacement cost valuation
      • 90% coinsurance
      • Building limit: $750,000
      • Covered fire loss: $200,000
      • Deductible: $5,000

      The insurance required is $1,000,000 × 90% = $900,000. The owner carries $750,000, so the requirement is not met.

      The coinsurance ratio is $750,000 ÷ $900,000 = 83.3%.

      The adjusted loss is $200,000 × 83.3% = $166,667. Subtracting the $5,000 deductible leaves an insurer payment of $161,667.

      If the building had been insured to the requirement, the payment would have been $200,000 − $5,000 = $195,000. The coinsurance penalty is $33,333, and the owner’s total out-of-pocket cost is $38,333: the $5,000 deductible plus the $33,333 penalty.

      To meet the requirement, the owner would need $150,000 of additional limit.

      Click Load Example in the calculator to see these numbers.

      Coinsurance at 80%, 90%, and 100%

      The coinsurance percentage changes the result even when nothing else does. The table below uses the same building, limit, loss, and deductible as the example above.

      A higher coinsurance percentage usually earns a lower rate per $100 of insurance, but it leaves less room for error in the property value. At 100%, any understatement of value creates a penalty.

      What Happens in a Total Loss

      Coinsurance mostly affects partial losses. If the same building at 90% coinsurance were destroyed, the calculation would be ($750,000 ÷ $900,000) × $1,000,000 − $5,000 = $828,333. That exceeds the limit, so the insurer pays the $750,000 limit. The coinsurance penalty on that loss is $0, but the owner still absorbs $250,000: the deductible plus $245,000 of loss above the limit. Underinsurance hurts in a total loss too, just through the limit rather than the coinsurance clause.

      How to Avoid a Coinsurance Penalty

      Start With an Accurate Replacement Cost

      Every other step depends on knowing what the property would cost to rebuild today. Property values reported at the original purchase, carried forward from an old statement of values, or based on market value are common sources of underinsurance. A replacement cost appraisal prepared by a qualified appraiser documents construction type, square footage, materials, and current local building costs, and it gives the underwriter a supported number.

      Agreed Value Optional Coverage

      The ISO commercial property form offers an Agreed Value optional coverage. When it is shown in the declarations, the coinsurance condition does not apply to that property until the expiration date listed for the agreed value. The insurer usually requires a signed statement of values to grant it.

      Two details matter. First, agreed value is tied to a time period and must be renewed; if it lapses, coinsurance applies again. Second, if the limit is less than the agreed value, the insurer pays only the proportion of the loss that the limit bears to the agreed value, which works much like a coinsurance penalty.

      Inflation Guard

      Inflation guard coverage increases the limit automatically by an annual percentage, prorated over the policy term. It helps a correctly set limit keep pace with rising costs during the year. It does not fix a limit that was too low at the start of the policy.

      Blanket Limits and Margin Clauses

      Owners with several buildings, or with building and contents at one location, can sometimes insure them under a single blanket limit instead of separate limits for each item. Under the ISO form, coinsurance on blanket insurance is applied to the combined value of all property under the blanket, which gives some flexibility when one building is underreported and another is overreported.

      Insurers often limit that flexibility with a margin clause. A margin clause caps what the policy will pay for any one building or location at a stated percentage of the value reported for it on the statement of values, for example 105% or 125%. A margin clause is a restriction, not a way to avoid coinsurance. It means an outdated statement of values can limit a recovery even when the total blanket limit is large. Blanket limits are most effective when the statement of values is current and agreed value is in force for the blanket.

      Review Values at Every Renewal

      Coinsurance is tested on the date of loss. Review the property value and limit at each renewal, after renovations or additions, and after periods of rapid construction cost growth.

      Coinsurance, Insurance to Value, and Appraisals

      Coinsurance is the policy language. Insurance to value is the practice that keeps you clear of it: carrying a limit equal to, or close to, the full replacement cost of the property.

      For condominium and homeowners associations, the stakes are shared. An underinsured master policy can turn a coinsurance penalty or a shortfall above the limit into a special assessment for every owner. Boards can check a building’s limit with our Condo Replacement Cost Calculator, and many associations rely on a periodic professional appraisal to support the values they report to their insurer.

      Coverage Estimate prepares replacement cost appraisals for insurance purposes. If the calculator shows a shortfall or a thin margin, contact us to discuss an appraisal before your next renewal.

      Common Coinsurance Mistakes

      Using Market Value or Purchase Price

      Market value includes land and location and can be far above or below construction cost. Coinsurance is based on the value of the covered property itself.

      Setting the Limit Once and Leaving It

      A limit that met the requirement at purchase can fall short years later as construction costs rise.

      Assuming the Clause Only Matters in a Total Loss

      The penalty applies to partial losses, which are the most common claims.

      Forgetting That Each Coverage Has Its Own Test

      Building, business personal property, and business income can each carry a separate coinsurance percentage and limit.

      Letting Agreed Value Lapse

      Agreed value usually lasts for a stated period. If it is not renewed, coinsurance returns without notice to most owners.

      Limitations of the Coinsurance Calculator

      The calculator is a screening tool. It does not:

      • Read or interpret your specific policy wording or endorsements
      • Determine the property value at the time of loss
      • Model forms that subtract the deductible before the coinsurance ratio
      • Apply sublimits, exclusions, or separate deductibles for wind, hail, or other perils
      • Model the homeowners replacement cost loss settlement provision
      • Calculate business income coinsurance, which uses a different worksheet
      • Determine whether a loss is covered

      When a large loss involves a coinsurance dispute, policyholders often work with a licensed public adjuster or attorney.

      Frequently Asked Questions

      What does 80% coinsurance mean?

      It means the policy requires a limit of at least 80% of the property’s value at the time of loss. On a building worth $1,000,000, the limit must be at least $800,000 to avoid a penalty.

      How is a coinsurance penalty calculated?

      Divide the limit carried by the insurance required, multiply the loss by that ratio, and subtract the deductible. The difference between that payment and what the loss would pay if fully insured is the penalty. Policy wording controls the exact order of steps.

      Is coinsurance the same in health insurance and property insurance?

      No. In health insurance, coinsurance is the share of medical costs you pay after the deductible. In property insurance, it is a clause requiring you to insure to a percentage of value. This calculator applies only to property insurance.

      Does coinsurance apply to a total loss?

      The clause still applies, but in most total losses the proportional payment exceeds the limit, so the insurer pays the limit. The owner absorbs the gap between the loss and the limit.

      How can I avoid a coinsurance penalty?

      Insure to an accurate, current replacement cost, ask about agreed value coverage, add inflation guard, keep the statement of values updated, and review the limit at every renewal.

      Do homeowners policies have coinsurance?

      Most standard homeowners policies do not have a coinsurance clause, but many include an 80% insurance-to-value test in their replacement cost loss settlement provision that can reduce payments in a similar way.

      Final Thoughts

      A coinsurance clause rewards accurate property values and penalizes outdated ones. The penalty rarely shows up until a claim, when it is too late to change the limit.

      Use the Coinsurance Calculator to test your current limit against the requirement on your declarations page, then try a few higher property values to see how much margin you have. If the result shows a penalty or a thin margin, confirm the property’s replacement cost and talk with your agent about the limit, agreed value, and inflation guard before your next renewal.

Estimate replacement cost, depreciation, and actual cash value for up to 25 items in a property insurance claim, plus your initial payment after the deductible and the recoverable depreciation you may collect after replacement.
